passages.happening:
The king of Jerusalem, Adoni-zedek, hears two things. Israel has taken Ai, and Gibeon has made peace with Israel. He and his people are ‘greatly alarmed, because Gibeon was a great city’ (verse 2).

He sends to four other kings, of Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish and Eglon: “Come up and help me. We will attack Gibeon, because they have made peace with Joshua and the Israelites” (verse 4). The five armies camp against Gibeon.

The men of Gibeon send to Joshua at Gilgal: ‘Do not abandon your servants. Come quickly and save us’ (verse 6).

Joshua goes up with the whole army. The LORD says to him, “Do not be afraid of them, for I have delivered them into your hand. Not one of them shall stand against you” (verse 8). After marching all night, Joshua takes the five armies by surprise (verse 9).

The LORD throws them into confusion. They flee down the road by Beth-horon, and as they run, ‘the LORD cast down on them large hailstones from the sky, and more of them were killed by the hailstones than by the swords of the Israelites’ (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
The five towns were real places in the south of the land. Jerusalem sat on the central ridge. Hebron lay to its south, and the other three in the low hills toward the coast. Letters written to Egypt's Pharaoh in the fourteenth century BC, found at Amarna, include some from a ruler of Jerusalem asking for help against his enemies. The Jerusalem of this chapter was that kind of small kingdom.

The five kings do not march on Israel. They march on Gibeon. A town that makes peace with Israel is a danger to all the others, and they mean to punish it.

So the first battle Israel fights after the treaty is a battle for the people who tricked it. Gibeon calls itself ‘your servants’ and asks for help, and Joshua does not hesitate. He could have let the five kings solve his problem for him. The oath had said only that Israel would let Gibeon live. Joshua treats it as a bond that makes Gibeon's danger his own. The promise that was won by a lie is kept at the cost of a night's forced march uphill.

Gilgal lay down in the Jordan valley, and Gibeon up in the hills. The army climbed through the dark and fought in the morning.

Then the writer takes care to say who won. The LORD confused the enemy. The LORD sent the hail. More died by hail than by Israel's swords. Israel marched hard and fought, and the book still counts the victory as God's.

The pass of Beth-horon was the main road between the hills and the coastal lowlands. Armies fought along it for centuries after.
passages.later:
Moses had told Israel at the Red Sea, “The LORD will fight for you; you need only to be still” (Exodus 14:14). This chapter says the same of this day: ‘the LORD fought for Israel’ (verse 14).

The Gibeonites remained under the protection of that oath long after. When King Saul broke it, the wrong was laid at his door (2 Samuel 21:1).
passages.asks: Joshua marched all night to rescue people who had lied to him, because he had given his word. Ask who has a claim on you that you would rather not honor because of how the tie began. Then notice that Israel marched all night and the book still says that God won the battle. Ask whether you can work with all your strength and still give God the credit.

passages.happening:
On the day of the battle Joshua speaks to the LORD in front of Israel:

“O sun, stand still over Gibeon, O moon, over the Valley of Aijalon” (verse 12).

The writer goes on: “So the sun stood still and the moon stopped until the nation took vengeance upon its enemies” (verse 13). He names his source, asking, ‘Is this not written in the Book of Jashar?’, and quotes it: “So the sun stopped in the middle of the sky and delayed going down about a full day” (verse 13).

Then he says what made the day unlike any other. “There has been no day like it before or since, when the LORD listened to the voice of a man, because the LORD fought for Israel” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
Joshua's words are set out as poetry, in two matching lines. The writer says they come from the Book of Jashar. That book seems to have been a collection of songs about Israel's heroes. It is quoted once more in the Bible, for David's lament over Saul and Jonathan, and it has not survived.

Gibeon stood on the high ground, and the Valley of Aijalon lay below it, at the foot of the Beth-horon road. The poem names the sun over one and the moon over the other.

The Hebrew verb translated ‘stand still’ can mean to be still, to be silent, or to stop. That is one reason readers have understood the lines in more than one way, as the hard question below sets out.

A reader should notice what the writer himself finds most astonishing. He does not say that there was never a day when the sky did such a thing. He says there was never a day ‘when the LORD listened to the voice of a man’ like this. The wonder he points to is the prayer and its answer. A man asked for something enormous, in front of the whole army, and God did it.

And he closes with the line that runs through the whole chapter: ‘because the LORD fought for Israel’.
passages.later:
The prophet Habakkuk, in a poem about God coming to save his people, uses the same picture: “Sun and moon stood still in their places at the flash of Your flying arrows, at the brightness of Your shining spear” (Habakkuk 3:11).

An older song in the book of Judges speaks of the sky joining a battle in a similar way: “From the heavens the stars fought; from their courses they fought against Sisera” (Judges 5:20).
passages.hard:
Did the sun really stand still?

Readers who receive this book as God's word take these verses in several ways.

Some understand them as a miracle in the sky itself. On this view God lengthened the day, whether by slowing the turning of the earth or by a local miracle of light. They point out that the text calls the day unique.

Others note that verses 12 and 13 are poetry, quoted from a book of songs. They read the lines as they read other poems in the Bible, such as the stars fighting against Sisera in Judges. On this view the words are vivid language for a day on which heaven itself seemed to fight for Israel.

Others have proposed that Joshua asked the sun and moon to stop shining and not to stop moving, so that the darkness of the hailstorm would go on. Some have compared the passage with texts from ancient Mesopotamia, which read the positions of the sun and moon as signs.

These notes do not choose among them. Each is held by careful readers, and each has to reckon with the words ‘about a full day’ and with the fact that the lines are a poem.

All of these readers agree on what the passage is for. It gives the credit for the victory to God, and it marvels that he listened to a man's voice.
passages.asks: The writer was most amazed that ‘the LORD listened to the voice of a man’. Ask what you have stopped asking God for because it seemed too large. Joshua asked out loud, where everyone could hear. Ask whether you ever pray in a way that would leave you exposed if nothing happened. And ask whose battle you are praying about, your own or God's.

passages.happening:
The five kings run and hide in a cave at Makkedah. Joshua has large stones rolled against its mouth and a guard set, and sends the army on after the fleeing soldiers (verses 16-19). The writer says that the pursuit was a great slaughter, and adds that ‘the remaining survivors retreated to the fortified cities’ (verse 20).

When the army is back in camp, Joshua has the kings brought out. He calls his commanders forward: “Come here and put your feet on the necks of these kings” (verse 24). Then he speaks to them: “Do not be afraid or discouraged,” Joshua said. “Be strong and courageous, for the LORD will do this to all the enemies you fight” (verse 25).

Joshua puts the kings to death and hangs their bodies on five trees until evening. At sunset they are taken down and put in the cave where they had hidden, and stones are set against its mouth (verses 26-27).
passages.hearers:
This passage is hard to read, and it is told briefly.

Placing a foot on the neck of a defeated king was a common sign of victory in the ancient world. It is shown in the carved pictures of Egypt and Assyria. It lies behind the Bible's picture of enemies made a footstool.

Joshua uses the moment to teach his officers. The words he gives them are the words God gave him in chapter 1, almost exactly: do not be afraid, be strong and courageous. The commander who needed to hear them now says them to others.

The bodies are hung up and taken down at sunset. This follows the law in Deuteronomy that a body hung on a tree must not be left overnight. Joshua did the same with the king of Ai. Even here the law sets a limit.

The cave that had been a hiding place becomes a grave. The stones at its mouth are another of the book's memorials, with the stones at the Jordan and the heap in the Valley of Achor. The writer says they could still be seen in his day.

One small phrase matters for reading the rest of the chapter. Verse 20 says that survivors got away to the walled cities. The verses that follow will say again and again that no survivors were left. The book puts both statements close together and does not seem troubled by it.

These are the acts of an ancient war, told as the ancient world told them. They are not held up for anyone to copy.
passages.later:
A psalm uses the footstool picture for the king God appoints: “The LORD said to my Lord: ‘Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet.’” (Psalm 110:1).

The New Testament applies that psalm to the risen Christ and names the enemies. They are not peoples. “For He must reign until He has put all His enemies under His feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death” (1 Corinthians 15:25-26).
passages.asks: Joshua passed on to his officers the very words that had once been spoken to him. Ask who gave you courage when you needed it, and who needs the same words from you now. Then read what Paul names as the last enemy. Ask what it changes to believe that the foes Christ puts under his feet are sin and death, and not other people.

passages.happening:
The rest of the chapter is a list, told in the same few phrases each time. Joshua takes Makkedah, then Libnah, then Lachish. The king of Gezer comes to help Lachish and is defeated. Then Eglon, Hebron and Debir. Of each town it is said that Israel put it to the sword, and of most that Joshua ‘devoted to destruction everyone in the city, leaving no survivors’ (verse 28).

Then comes a summary of the whole southern campaign. Joshua conquered the hill country, the Negev, the foothills and the slopes. ‘He devoted to destruction everything that breathed, just as the LORD, the God of Israel, had commanded’ (verse 40).

The writer gives the reason for the speed of it: “And because the LORD, the God of Israel, fought for Israel, Joshua captured all these kings and their land in one campaign” (verse 42). Then the army goes back to the camp at Gilgal (verse 43).
passages.hearers:
The writing changes here. The stories of Rahab, Achan and Gibeon were full of people and speech. This passage is a report, with the same sentence repeated for town after town. It moves quickly and does not describe what it reports.

The repeated words have to be taken seriously. They say that whole towns were destroyed, and the summary uses the words of the command in Deuteronomy: everything that breathed. This is the same hard matter as Jericho.

The book also gives a careful reader things to set beside those words. Verse 20, a few lines earlier, says that survivors reached the walled cities. Hebron and Debir are said here to have been wiped out, and yet in chapter 15 Caleb has to take both of them from the people living there. The king of Jerusalem is killed in this chapter, and yet the book says later that the people of Jerusalem could not be driven out. And three chapters on, God tells Joshua that very much of the land is still not taken.

Kings across the ancient world told of their wars in the same kind of language. Records from Egypt and Assyria say that enemies were wiped out and no one was left, sometimes of victories that were far from complete. A king of Moab claimed on his monument that Israel had perished for ever. The phrase ‘leaving no survivors’ belongs to that stock of expressions. Many scholars, evangelical scholars among them, read Joshua's summaries in that light. Others take them more literally. The hard question says more.

The passage ends as each part of this chapter has ended, with the statement that the LORD fought for Israel. The book never lets Israel take the credit.
passages.later:
The command the summary quotes is in Deuteronomy: “you must not leave alive anything that breathes” (Deuteronomy 20:16).

The book's own later words stand beside the summary: ‘very much of the land remains to be possessed’ (Joshua 13:1), and “But the descendants of Judah could not drive out the Jebusites living in Jerusalem” (Joshua 15:63).

The prophet Isaiah looked ahead to the end of all such campaigns: “They will beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning hooks. Nation will no longer take up the sword against nation, nor train anymore for war” (Isaiah 2:4).
passages.hard:
The chapter says again and again that Joshua left no survivors. How should a reader take that?

There are two questions here, one about what happened and one about whether it was right.

On what happened, the book itself supplies the difficulty. It says that no one survived, and it says that survivors fled to the walled cities (verse 20) and that Hebron, Debir and Jerusalem still had to be dealt with later. Many scholars conclude that the summaries follow the customs of ancient reports of war, which used sweeping phrases of total victory. Others take the statements more literally and explain the later notes as towns that were settled again. These notes do not choose.

On whether it was right, the note on chapter 6, verses 17 to 21, sets out the readings Christians hold and the cost of each. Some read these wars as God's judgment on particular peoples at one moment, after long patience (Genesis 15:16). Some read the sweeping words as the idiom of their age. Some ground the command in God's right over life. Some read these chapters as a stage in what Israel understood of God, to be read in the light of Christ. Many hold more than one together. No one of these answers satisfies every reader, and the difficulty is real.

One thing is not in doubt. No one may use this chapter to justify violence against any person or people. It tells of towns and peoples of the ancient world. It says nothing about any nation, state, land or conflict today.

The site's pages on the violence of the Old Testament and on the command to destroy the Canaanites go further.
passages.asks: Do not let the repeated phrases slide past. Ask what you feel when you read them, and tell God. Ask whether you have ever heard a passage like this used to make cruelty sound holy, and what you would say to that now. Then notice the line the chapter keeps repeating about who fought. Ask where you are taking credit that is not yours.
